db_pool_exhaustion.title: Database connection pool exhaustion after payments deploy

trigger_deploy.change_summary: Increase payment authorization retries from 3 to 5 and hold the DB transaction open across retries

fix_deploy.change_summary: Rollback to <<ver_old>> (<<inc>>: Database connection pool exhaustion after payments deploy)

runbook.content: Checkout and payment requests time out or return 503 while acquiring a database connection. Postgres logs show 'too many clients already' (SQLSTATE 53300). Connection count on the primary sits at or near max_connections. Error rate climbs within minutes of a deploy to a service that talks to the primary.

Alerts: PostgresConnectionsHigh (warning at 90%), PostgresConnectionsExhausted (critical at 100%), CheckoutErrorRateHigh. Dashboard: Postgres Primary > Connections by application_name. A single application_name owning most connections points to the culprit service.

Run SELECT application_name, state, count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity GROUP BY 1,2 ORDER BY 3 DESC. Look for many 'idle in transaction' sessions from one app. Check the deploy timeline for that service in the last 30 minutes. Compare the new version's connection handling: transactions held across external calls or retries are the usual cause.

Roll back the offending service to the previous version first; do not try to fix forward during the incident. If the primary is still saturated after rollback, terminate idle-in-transaction sessions older than 60s with pg_terminate_backend. As a last resort raise max_connections temporarily, but this needs a restart and shifts the problem to memory.
Connections on the primary drop below 60% within two minutes of rollback. CheckoutErrorRateHigh resolves. Checkout p99 returns under 800ms. Confirm no lingering idle-in-transaction sessions.

Page data-infra if the primary does not recover after rollback and session termination. Page payments-platform lead if rollback itself fails. Open a SEV1 if checkout availability is below 95% for more than 10 minutes.

Alerts associated with this failure mode: CheckoutErrorRateHigh, PaymentsLatencyP99, PostgresConnectionsExhausted, PostgresConnectionsHigh. Primary error code in logs: PG_53300. Owning team: payments-platform. Services typically involved: checkout-api, payments, postgres.

postmortem.content: SEV1 incident on <<date>> lasting <<duration>> minutes in <<region>>. Database connection pool exhaustion after payments deploy. The trigger was deployment <<dep>> to payments. Incident commander: <<commander>> (<<team>>). Services affected: checkout-api, payments, postgres.

<<t1>> UTC first anomalous signals in checkout-api logs. <<t2>> first critical alert fires; <<commander>> acknowledges and declares <<inc>> as SEV1. <<t3>> root cause hypothesis formed from logs and deploy timeline. <<t4>> mitigation applied. <<t5>> alerts resolved and incident marked mitigated. Postmortem published <<pm_date>>.

A payments deploy changed the authorization flow to retry the payment processor up to five times while holding the surrounding database transaction open. Under normal processor latency each request now held a connection for several seconds instead of tens of milliseconds, and the pool of 50 per replica across 12 replicas saturated the primary's max_connections of 500 within minutes.

The change was reviewed for correctness of the retry logic but not for connection hold time. Staging runs with 2 replicas and a processor stub that returns instantly, so pool pressure never appeared in pre-production. No connection-pool-utilization alert existed at the service level; the first alert fired from Postgres at 90%. Checkout-api shares the same primary and had no bulkhead, so an unrelated service's connection use took it down.
Checkout success rate dropped to <<n>>% for <<duration>> minutes. Approximately <<n>> checkout attempts failed or timed out. Payments already authorized were not affected.

1. Move payment processor retries outside the database transaction boundary.; 2. Add per-service pool utilization alert at 80% (owner: payments-platform).; 3. Introduce PgBouncer in transaction pooling mode in front of the primary (owner: data-infra).; 4. Add a load test stage to the payments pipeline that exercises processor latency (owner: payments-platform).. Tracked as GitHub issues labeled postmortem-action-item and linked to <<inc>>.

issues.title: Authorization retries hold DB transaction open, exhausting connection pool
issues.body:
During <<inc>> the retry loop added in <<dep>> kept the transaction open for the whole retry sequence. With processor p50 around 800ms and up to 5 attempts, a single request held a connection for 4s+.

Proposed fix: authorize outside the transaction, then open a short transaction to persist the result. Also cap retries at 3 with a 2s total budget.

See postmortem <<inc>> for timeline.

issues.title: Deploy PgBouncer in transaction mode in front of tigerlily-primary
issues.body:
Action item from <<inc>>. Every app service opens its own pool directly against the primary, so one misbehaving service can take everyone down. A transaction-mode pooler caps server connections at a fixed number and lets us give each service a bounded share.

Open questions: prepared statement handling for the Java services, and whether we lose LISTEN/NOTIFY for notifications.

tls_cert_expiry.title: Expired TLS certificate on edge proxy

runbook.content: Clients fail to connect with 'certificate has expired'. Backend services look healthy and quiet: request volume drops sharply while error rates inside the cluster stay at zero. Synthetic probes fail at the TLS layer before any HTTP request is sent.

Alerts: CertificateExpiringSoon (warning at 14 days), CertificateExpired (critical), EdgeTLSHandshakeFailures, TrafficDropAnomaly. Quick check: openssl s_client -connect api.tigerlily.example:443 -servername api.tigerlily.example | openssl x509 -noout -dates.

Check cert-manager logs for the Certificate resource: kubectl describe certificate api-tigerlily-tls -n edge. Renewal usually failed for a mundane reason: the ACME HTTP-01 challenge path is blocked by a WAF rule or routing change, DNS for the domain changed, or the issuer secret was rotated. Note that a renewal that has been failing for weeks still only pages at expiry if the warning alert is unrouted.

Fix the underlying renewal blocker (most often: allow /.well-known/acme-challenge/ through the WAF and edge routes), then force a renewal with cmctl renew api-tigerlily-tls. If ACME cannot be fixed quickly, upload the emergency backup certificate from the secrets vault and reload the proxy. Never disable TLS verification on clients.
openssl s_client shows a notAfter date in the future. EdgeTLSHandshakeFailures drops to zero. Request volume at api-gateway returns to baseline within five minutes as clients reconnect.
Page platform-infra immediately; this is a full outage of the public API. If the ACME issuer is down, contact the certificate vendor. Open a SEV1.

Alerts associated with this failure mode: CertificateExpired, CertificateExpiringSoon, EdgeTLSHandshakeFailures, TrafficDropAnomaly. Primary error code in logs: CERT_EXPIRED. Owning team: platform-infra. Services typically involved: edge-proxy, api-gateway.

postmortem.content: SEV1 incident on <<date>> lasting <<duration>> minutes in <<region>>. Expired TLS certificate on edge proxy. Incident commander: <<commander>> (<<team>>). Services affected: edge-proxy, api-gateway.

<<t1>> UTC first anomalous signals in edge-proxy logs. <<t2>> first critical alert fires; <<commander>> acknowledges and declares <<inc>> as SEV1. <<t3>> root cause hypothesis formed from logs and deploy timeline. <<t4>> mitigation applied. <<t5>> alerts resolved and incident marked mitigated. Postmortem published <<pm_date>>.

The edge TLS certificate for api.tigerlily.example expired. cert-manager had been attempting renewal for 19 days, but the ACME HTTP-01 challenge was blocked by a WAF rule added to stop path-scanning bots, which matched /.well-known/acme-challenge/ as a suspicious path. The CertificateExpiringSoon warning fired to a Slack channel nobody was watching.

The WAF rule change was tested against application routes, not against the ACME challenge path. CertificateExpiringSoon was routed to a low-traffic Slack channel rather than the on-call pager. No synthetic monitor checked certificate validity independently of cert-manager's own status.
The public API was unreachable for all clients with correct certificate validation for <<duration>> minutes. Web and mobile checkout were fully unavailable. Backend services were unaffected.

1. Route CertificateExpiringSoon to the platform-infra pager at 14 and 7 days.; 2. Add an explicit WAF allow rule for /.well-known/acme-challenge/ and a test in the WAF rule CI.; 3. Add an external synthetic check that asserts certificate notAfter is more than 10 days out.; 4. Store an emergency certificate in the vault and document the manual rotation path.. Tracked as GitHub issues labeled postmortem-action-item and linked to <<inc>>.

issues.title: WAF rule 942100 blocks ACME HTTP-01 challenge path, breaking certificate renewal
issues.body:
Root cause of <<inc>>. The path-scanning rule added to block /.well-known/ enumeration also blocked cert-manager's HTTP-01 challenge. Renewal failed silently for 19 days.

Fix: explicit allow for /.well-known/acme-challenge/ evaluated before the deny rules, plus a CI test that issues a challenge-style request through the WAF config.

issues.title: Route certificate expiry warnings to pager, not Slack
issues.body: CertificateExpiringSoon fired daily for two weeks before <<inc>> into #infra-notifications. Nobody saw it. Proposal: warning to pager at 14 days (business hours), critical at 7 days (24x7).

embedding_worker_oom.title: Embedding worker OOMKilled after model rollout

trigger_deploy.change_summary: Roll out product embedding model v3 (1024-dim, larger vocabulary) for similar-items

runbook.content: Embedding worker pods restart repeatedly with exit code 137 and reason OOMKilled. Consumer lag on catalog.product-updated grows because batches never commit. Recommendations serve popularity fallbacks and similar-items quality degrades. Nothing is 'down' from the user's point of view, which makes this easy to miss.

Alerts: PodCrashLooping in namespace discovery, KafkaConsumerLagHigh for group embedding-worker. Dashboard: Discovery > Embedding pipeline > RSS by pod, and the 'embedding coverage' panel on the recommendations board.

kubectl describe pod on a restarted worker shows Last State: Terminated, Reason: OOMKilled. Check what changed: a new model (larger weights or vocabulary), a larger batch size, or a dependency upgrade that changed tensor memory behavior. Model weights plus one batch of activations must fit under the container limit with headroom; with v3 a 256-item batch alone needs about 1.4GB.

Reduce batch_size via the BATCH_SIZE env var (32 is safe for v3) and raise the memory limit to 4Gi. Either alone may be enough; do both during the incident. If the model itself is the problem, roll back to the previous model tag. The pipeline is idempotent, so lag drains on its own once workers stay up.
No new OOMKilled events for 15 minutes. Consumer lag trending toward zero. Embedding coverage on the recommendations dashboard returns above 99%.
Page discovery on-call. If lag exceeds 100k messages, coordinate with data-infra on Kafka retention so offsets are not lost.

postmortem.content: SEV2 incident on <<date>> lasting <<duration>> minutes in <<region>>. Embedding worker OOMKilled after model rollout. The trigger was deployment <<dep>> to embedding-worker. Incident commander: <<commander>> (<<team>>). Services affected: embedding-worker, recommendations.

<<t1>> UTC first anomalous signals in embedding-worker logs. <<t2>> first critical alert fires; <<commander>> acknowledges and declares <<inc>> as SEV2. <<t3>> root cause hypothesis formed from logs and deploy timeline. <<t4>> mitigation applied. <<t5>> alerts resolved and incident marked mitigated. Postmortem published <<pm_date>>.

The product-embed-v3 model rollout increased weight size from 420MB to 910MB and embedding dimension from 768 to 1024. With the unchanged batch size of 256, peak working memory rose above the 2GB container limit, and the kernel killed the container mid-batch. Because the batch never committed its Kafka offset, each restart replayed the same batch and died at the same point.

Memory limits were set for the v2 model and not revisited during the v3 rollout. The model card documented weight size but not peak inference memory at the production batch size. Staging processes a tiny catalog and never reached a full 256-item batch. PodCrashLooping in the discovery namespace was a warning, not a page.

Similar-items recommendations degraded to popularity fallback for <<n>>% of product pages over <<n>> minutes. No errors visible to shoppers. Estimated recommendation click-through dropped by roughly a third during the window.

1. Add peak memory at production batch size to the model rollout checklist.; 2. Make batch size adaptive to available memory in the worker.; 3. Promote PodCrashLooping in discovery to a page during business hours.; 4. Add a staging soak that processes at least 10 full batches before promotion.. Tracked as GitHub issues labeled postmortem-action-item and linked to <<inc>>.

issues.title: embedding-worker OOMKilled with product-embed-v3 at batch_size=256
issues.body:
From <<inc>>. v3 roughly doubled resident memory per batch. Workers died with exit 137 and replayed the same offsets on restart.

Short term (done during incident): batch_size=32, limit 4Gi.
Longer term: size batches from available memory at startup, and add a memory regression check to the model promotion pipeline.

issues.title: Commit Kafka offsets per sub-batch so a crash does not replay the whole batch
issues.body: During <<inc>> every restart replayed 256 messages and died at the same spot, so lag never moved. Committing after each 32-item sub-batch would bound the replay and let a struggling worker make progress.

bad_deploy_npe.title: Catalog API regression returning 500s after deploy

trigger_deploy.change_summary: Refactor variant pricing lookup to use the new price_history table

fix_deploy.change_summary: Rollback to <<ver_old>> (<<inc>>: Catalog API regression returning 500s after deploy)

runbook.content: A sharp step change in 5xx rate for one service that lines up with a deploy. Stack traces all point at the same new code path. Downstream callers (gateway, cart) show correlated 500s or fall back to stale cache.

Alerts: <Service>ErrorRateHigh, GatewayUpstream5xx. The deploy annotation on the error-rate graph makes the correlation obvious. Canary analysis should have caught it; check whether the canary threshold was too loose or the affected endpoint received too little canary traffic.

Pull the top exception signature from logs for the service in the last 15 minutes. If a single new stack frame dominates and the deploy is under an hour old, stop diagnosing and roll back. Root-cause analysis happens after the rollback.

Roll back to the previous version using the deploy tool: tigerlily-deploy rollback <service> --to <prev_version>. Do not hotfix forward during the incident. If the rollback is blocked by a schema migration, page the service lead.
Error rate returns to baseline within one rollout cycle (two to three minutes). Downstream 5xx alerts resolve. Spot-check the failing endpoint manually.
Page the owning team. Open a SEV2 if error rate exceeds 10% or a SEV1 if checkout is affected.

A refactor moved variant pricing to the new price_history table but assumed every variant had at least one history row. Roughly 8% of variants, mostly newly created ones, had no row yet, and the lookup dereferenced a null result. Canary analysis passed because the 10% canary slice received few requests for those variants in its five-minute window.

The backfill migration for price_history was scheduled to run after the code deploy rather than before. Canary promotion used an error-rate threshold of 5%, which the canary stayed under during its short window. Unit tests covered variants with history but no test covered a missing-history variant.

issues.title: NPE in PricingResolver when variant has no price_history row
issues.body:
Cause of <<inc>>. PricingResolver.resolve assumes a non-empty history list. About 8% of variants have none (created after the last backfill).

Fix: fall back to variant.base_price and log at debug. Add a unit test for the empty case. Backfill should run before the next deploy of this path.

issues.title: Canary promotion threshold too permissive (5% error rate, 5 min)

dns_resolution_failure.title: Cluster DNS failures causing intermittent upstream timeouts

runbook.content: Intermittent 502 and 504 errors across many unrelated services at once. Error messages mention 'no such host', 'server misbehaving', 'i/o timeout' on .svc.cluster.local names. The services being called look perfectly healthy in their own logs. Errors are bursty rather than constant.

Alerts: CoreDNSErrorRate, GatewayUpstream5xx firing for several upstreams together. Dashboard: Platform > Cluster DNS. If many services fail at the same time with no shared deploy, suspect DNS or networking before application code.

kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l k8s-app=kube-dns. Fewer ready replicas than expected, or all replicas on one node, is the usual finding after node maintenance. Check CoreDNS logs for SERVFAIL or upstream timeouts. From a debug pod, run dig payments.svc.cluster.local repeatedly to see the failure rate.

Scale CoreDNS back to at least 3 replicas spread across nodes. Restart CoreDNS pods if they are ready but returning SERVFAIL. Enable NodeLocal DNSCache if it is not on. Application teams should not change anything during the incident; their retries will succeed once DNS recovers.
dig from a debug pod succeeds 100 times in a row. CoreDNSErrorRate resolves. Gateway 5xx returns to baseline within two minutes.
Page platform-infra. If the cluster network itself is degraded (CNI errors, node NotReady), page the cloud provider support line.

Alerts associated with this failure mode: CoreDNSErrorRate, GatewayUpstream5xx. Primary error code in logs: DNS_NXDOMAIN. Owning team: platform-infra. Services typically involved: api-gateway, checkout-api, payments, search-api.

A node pool rotation for a kernel patch drained nodes one at a time. Add CoreDNS ready-replica count to the pre-flight checks of the node rotation runbook.. Tracked as GitHub issues labeled postmortem-action-item and linked to <<inc>>.

kafka_consumer_lag.title: Order fulfillment backlog from Kafka consumer lag

runbook.content: Orders are accepted but fulfillment and confirmation emails lag by many minutes. Consumer lag on orders.created climbs steadily. The consumer group may rebalance repeatedly. Nothing errors; it is a throughput problem.
Alerts: KafkaConsumerLagHigh (warning), KafkaConsumerLagCritical (oldest message age over 10 minutes). Dashboard: Fulfillment > Order pipeline > lag by partition and processing rate.

Determine whether producers sped up (a sale, a bot) or consumers slowed down (a slow downstream such as inventory reserve, a slow DB, GC pauses). Compare messages-in per second with messages-processed per second. Check whether the HPA is pinned at max replicas. Note that consumer replicas beyond the partition count do nothing; 6 partitions means at most 6 active consumers.

If consumers are slow because of a downstream, fix or bypass the downstream first. Otherwise scale: raise HPA max, raise per-consumer concurrency, and if partitions are the ceiling, add partitions (this is irreversible and changes key-to-partition mapping, so coordinate with the service owner). Communicate the delay to support so customers are told.
Lag trending down consistently for ten minutes. Oldest message age under two minutes. Email backlog drained.
Page fulfillment on-call. If lag exceeds retention risk (millions of messages), page data-infra to extend topic retention before offsets expire.

redis_eviction_storm.title: Redis eviction storm causing cart data loss

runbook.content: Shoppers report empty carts. cart-service logs show cache misses, rebuilds, and 404s for guest carts. Redis used_memory sits at maxmemory and evicted_keys climbs. Postgres load rises as carts are rebuilt.
Alerts: RedisMemoryHigh, RedisEvictionRateHigh, CartNotFoundRateHigh. Dashboard: Storefront > Cart > cache hit rate, and Data > Redis > memory and evictions.

Run INFO memory and INFO stats on the cache primary. If evicted_keys is rising, find what grew: redis-cli --bigkeys or the keyspace panel by prefix. Correlate with recent flag flips or deploys that changed TTLs or added a new key family. Guest carts live only in Redis, so their eviction is data loss.

Stop the growth first (revert the flag or deploy that changed TTLs). Raise maxmemory if the instance has headroom. Reduce TTL on the offending prefix with a SCAN loop rather than FLUSH. Do not switch eviction policy to noeviction during an incident; writes will start failing instead.
evicted_keys stays at zero for ten minutes. Cache hit rate above 95%. CartNotFoundRateHigh resolves.
Page data-infra for Redis capacity changes. Page storefront for the application side.

postmortem.content: SEV2 incident on <<date>> lasting <<duration>> minutes in <<region>>. Redis eviction storm causing cart data loss. Incident commander: <<commander>> (<<team>>). Services affected: redis-cache, cart-service.

<<t1>> UTC first anomalous signals in redis-cache logs. <<t2>> first critical alert fires; <<commander>> acknowledges and declares <<inc>> as SEV2. <<t3>> root cause hypothesis formed from logs and deploy timeline. <<t4>> mitigation applied. <<t5>> alerts resolved and incident marked mitigated. A feature flag extended guest cart TTL from 2 hours to 30 days to improve return-visit conversion. Guest carts are the largest keyspace in the shared cache, and with the longer TTL the working set grew past maxmemory within a day. The allkeys-lru policy then evicted active carts along with stale ones, and guest carts have no persistent copy.

Guest carts were stored only in Redis, so eviction meant loss. The flag change was treated as a product experiment and did not go through capacity review. The shared cache mixed session, cart, and catalog keys with a single eviction policy.
Approximately <<n>> guest carts were lost and <<n>>% of cart reads returned <<n>> for <<duration>> minutes. Logged-in carts were rebuilt from Postgres with elevated latency.

1. Persist guest carts to Postgres with a 30-day retention job.; 2. Split cart keys into a dedicated Redis instance with volatile-lru.; 3. Require capacity review for flags that change TTLs or key cardinality.. Tracked as GitHub issues labeled postmortem-action-item and linked to <<inc>>.

issues.body: Carts share cache-primary with sessions and catalog fragments. Move cart:* to its own instance with volatile-lru so eviction pressure from one keyspace cannot affect the others. From <<inc>>.

runbook.content: Writes fail with 'No space left on device' (SQLSTATE 53100). In the worst case the primary PANICs and restarts. Before that, disk usage on the WAL volume climbs steadily for hours or days while data volume stays flat.
Alerts: PostgresDiskUsageHigh at 80%, PostgresDiskUsageCritical at 95%, PostgresPrimaryDown. Dashboard: Data > Postgres > WAL size and archive lag. Also watch pg_replication_slots for inactive slots.

WAL grows when something prevents it from being recycled: an inactive replication slot holding restart_lsn, a failing archive_command, or a long-running transaction. Run SELECT slot_name, active, pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), restart_lsn)) FROM pg_replication_slots. Check the log for archive failures. Check pg_stat_archiver.

Free space without deleting WAL files by hand. Drop or advance the inactive slot if the replica is gone for good. Fix the archive command (credentials, bucket permissions) so pending segments ship. If the disk is already full, expand the volume online first, then fix the cause. Never rm files from pg_wal.
pg_wal size shrinks after the next checkpoint. pg_stat_archiver last_archived_time is recent. Disk usage under 50%. Application error rates back to baseline.
Page data-infra immediately at the critical alert. If the primary does not come back after restart, begin failover to the standby per the failover runbook.

runbook.content: A service's memory climbs steadily from startup until it is OOMKilled, restarts, and climbs again. The sawtooth is visible over hours. Latency degrades toward the top of each cycle as GC works harder. Users see occasional 502s and slow searches rather than an outage.

processor_rate_limit.title: Payment processor rate limiting during retry storm

runbook.content: Payment authorizations fail with 429 from the processor. It usually starts with a brief processor blip (503s or slow responses); our retries then multiply the request rate past the account limit and the processor throttles us for minutes after it has recovered. Checkout shows 'payment unavailable'.
Alerts: ProcessorErrorRateHigh, PaymentAuthorizationFailures, CheckoutErrorRateHigh. Dashboard: Payments > Processor > requests, retries, and 429s. Check the processor's status page.

Look at the ratio of retries to first attempts in outbound processor calls. If retries dominate, we are amplifying the problem. Check whether the client honors Retry-After. Check the number of payments replicas: each has its own retry budget, and they multiply.

Open the circuit breaker so we stop hammering the processor, then let it half-open and probe. Reduce retries to a small budget with jittered backoff. If the processor remains degraded for long, switch to the secondary processor per the processor-failover runbook. Ask support to message affected customers that pending payments will settle.
429 rate at zero. Authorization success above 99%. Billing reconcile job reports zero authorizations stuck in UNKNOWN.
Page payments-platform. Open a ticket with the processor if their status page shows an incident. SEV1 if checkout failure exceeds 10% for 10 minutes.

runbook.content: Pods across unrelated namespaces are Evicted with 'The node was low on resource: memory'. New pods fail scheduling with Insufficient memory. Deployments run below desired replicas. Services with few replicas see errors; services with many see latency.
Alerts: NodeMemoryPressure, DeploymentReplicasUnavailable, PodEvictedRate. Dashboard: Platform > Nodes > allocatable vs used, and pods without limits.

The culprit is almost always a pod with no memory limit that grew, or a burst of pods scheduled by requests alone. Look for a batch job or bulk import that started around the same time.

Stop or cap the pod that is consuming the node (set a limit, scale it down, pause the job). Add nodes if the pool is near allocatable. Evicted pods reschedule on their own once memory frees. Clear any locks held by evicted jobs.

mtls_cert_mismatch.title: mTLS handshake failures between auth-service and user-profile

runbook.content: One service cannot call another over the mesh: 'certificate signed by unknown authority' or 'unknown_ca' TLS alerts. The callee looks healthy and serves other callers fine. Symptoms appear during or shortly after a mesh CA rotation or a sidecar upgrade.
Alerts: UpstreamTLSFailures (per source/dest pair), plus the caller's own error-rate alert. Dashboard: Platform > Mesh > handshake failures by pair.

Compare the trust bundle on the caller's sidecar with the issuer of the callee's workload certificate. During a CA rotation the new root must be in every trust bundle before any workload certificate is issued by the new CA. A partial rollout that rotates workload certs in some namespaces before trust bundles in others produces exactly this.

Push the new root into the caller's trust bundle (both roots must be present during rotation) and restart the caller's sidecars. Do not disable mTLS or set permissive mode on tier-1 services during the incident unless the CA infrastructure itself is broken.
Handshake failures for the pair drop to zero. Caller error rate resolves. Every sidecar in the mesh reports both roots in its bundle.

migration_lock.title: Schema migration lock blocking inventory writes

trigger_deploy.change_summary: Migration 0142: add NOT NULL column warehouse_id with default to inventory_levels

runbook.content: Writes to one table stall then fail with lock timeouts (SQLSTATE 55P03). Reads may continue. A migration is running. Lock waits pile up and connections are consumed by waiting sessions, so other tables can be affected indirectly.
Alerts: PostgresLockWaitsHigh, the owning service's error-rate alert. Query: SELECT pid, wait_event_type, state, left(query, 80) FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE wait_event_type = 'Lock'.

Find the blocker with SELECT pg_blocking_pids(pid) or the pg_locks join in the DBA snippets. If the blocker is the migrator role holding AccessExclusiveLock on a big table, the migration is doing a full rewrite (adding a column with a volatile default, changing a type, adding NOT NULL without a validated constraint) or is queued behind a long transaction and holding the lock while it waits.

Cancel the migration with pg_cancel_backend; use pg_terminate_backend if cancel does not work within 10 seconds. The table returns to its previous state. Rewrite the migration to be online: add the column nullable, backfill in batches, add a NOT VALID check constraint and validate separately, then set NOT NULL. Always set lock_timeout to a few seconds in migration sessions.
No processes waiting on the relation. Service error rate at baseline. Migration marked as not applied so it can be rerun safely.
Page data-infra if the blocker cannot be identified or cancelled. Page the owning service team.

clock_skew_jwt.title: Clock skew causing JWT validation failures

runbook.content: Freshly issued tokens are rejected as 'not yet valid' or 'expired' by some gateway replicas but not others. Users are logged out or asked to re-authenticate repeatedly. Token refresh traffic spikes. The auth service itself reports no errors.
Alerts: Gateway401RateHigh, NodeClockSkew, AuthTokenRefreshStorm. Dashboard: Platform > Nodes > clock offset.

Compare 'date' across gateway nodes and the auth-service nodes. If offsets exceed a second, find out why NTP stopped syncing: chrony logs will show unreachable sources, which usually means a network policy or firewall change blocked udp/123. Restore NTP reachability and let chrony step the clock (or restart chronyd with makestep). As a stop-gap raise the validator's clock skew tolerance to 30 seconds. Do not disable nbf or exp validation.

autoscaler_flapping.title: HPA flapping on api-gateway causing latency spikes

runbook.content: Replica count oscillates every minute or two. Latency spikes coincide with scale events as new replicas serve traffic before their connection pools and caches are warm. Error rate stays low but p99 is terrible.
Alerts: HPAFlapping (more than 4 rescales in 15 minutes), GatewayLatencyP99. Dashboard: replica count overlaid on p99.

kubectl describe hpa shows the rescale events and reasons. Look for a recent change to target utilization, stabilization window, or metrics. A target set too close to idle CPU, combined with a zero stabilization window, guarantees oscillation: scale up drops per-pod CPU below target, scale down raises it above.

Restore a scale-down stabilization window of at least 300 seconds and a sane target (60% for the gateway). Raise minReplicas so warm-up cost is amortized. If flapping is severe, temporarily pin replicas by removing the HPA and setting a fixed count.
Replica count stable for 30 minutes. p99 under SLO.

poison_message.title: Poison message stalling the notifications consumer

runbook.content: One partition's lag grows while the others stay flat. The consumer logs the same exception at the same offset repeatedly. Downstream effects hit only a subset of users (those whose keys hash to the stuck partition).
Alerts: ConsumerPartitionStalled (offset unchanged for N minutes with lag), KafkaConsumerLagHigh. Dashboard: lag by partition.

Read the message at the stuck offset with kcat or the Kafka UI. Usually it fails schema validation or deserialization, often because a producer shipped a schema change first. Check which producer build wrote it.

Copy the message to the DLQ topic and advance the consumer group's offset past it (kafka-consumer-groups --reset-offsets --to-offset for that partition, with the group stopped). Then stop the producer from emitting more, by rollback or hotfix. Long term the consumer must route undeserializable messages to the DLQ automatically.
Offset advancing on the partition. Lag draining. No new parse errors.
Owning team. Coordinate with the producer's team for the schema fix.

replica_lag_stale_reads.title: Read replica lag causing stale order status

runbook.content: Customers see out-of-date order status or profile data. Writes succeed but reads do not reflect them for seconds to minutes. Replica replay lag is high. Some replica queries are cancelled with 'conflict with recovery'.
Alerts: PostgresReplicaLagHigh (30s), PostgresReplicaLagCritical (300s), OrderStatusStaleReads. Query on replica: SELECT now() - pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp().

Determine whether the replica is receiving WAL but not applying it (replay lag with low flush lag: a long query on the replica is blocking apply, or apply is CPU/IO bound) or not receiving it (network, primary WAL sender). Check what is generating WAL on the primary: a bulk backfill or a large VACUUM is typical.

Pause the WAL-heavy job on the primary. Cancel long queries on the replica if hot_standby_feedback is off and they block apply. Route read-your-own-writes paths (order status, profile after edit) to the primary until lag recovers. Do not promote the replica.
Replay lag under 1 second. Stale-read sample rate at zero. Backfill resumed at a throttled rate.

postmortem.content: SEV1 incident on <<date>> lasting <<duration>> minutes in <<region>>. Feature flag rollout to 100% enabling broken checkout path. Incident commander: <<commander>> (<<team>>). Services affected: checkout-api, payments.

<<t1>> UTC first anomalous signals in checkout-api logs. <<t2>> first critical alert fires; <<commander>> acknowledges and declares <<inc>> as SEV1. <<t3>> root cause hypothesis formed from logs and deploy timeline. <<t4>> mitigation applied. <<t5>> alerts resolved and incident marked mitigated. Postmortem published <<pm_date>>.

The checkout-express-v2 flag was meant to move from 5% to 25% for US customers only. The operator changed the percentage to 100% and removed the country rule in the same edit. The express path had no tax provider configured for non-US regions and its address normalizer failed on several postal code formats, so most non-US checkouts errored.

The flag UI allowed percentage and targeting rules to change in one step with no confirmation for tier-1 flags. No guardrail metric (error rate per variant) was attached to the flag. Express v2 had only been tested with US addresses.
Roughly <<n>>% of non-US checkouts failed for <<duration>> minutes, about <<n>> orders. US checkouts were unaffected.

1. Require two-person approval for tier-1 flag changes over 25% or that remove targeting rules.; 2. Attach an automatic guardrail: revert the flag if variant error rate exceeds 2x control for <<duration>> minutes.; 3. Add non-US address fixtures to express v2 tests.. Tracked as GitHub issues labeled postmortem-action-item and linked to <<inc>>.
